title: Verify and De-risk Workshop (Lab)
summary: Groups apply a fixed four-step verification routine to a batch of suspect outputs, record an evidence-backed verdict for each, then compare single-source and two-source checking to judge which is more reliable.
objectives: Apply a verification routine to a set of suspect outputs and record the verdict for each.
Compare two verification strategies and judge which is more reliable.

sections.heading: Verify and De-risk Workshop (Lab)
body: One suspect output is easy to check. Ten is where you need a system. Today you run a verification routine on a whole batch, reach an evidence-backed verdict on each, and then judge which checking strategy you would actually trust.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can run a verification routine on several suspect outputs and record a clear verdict for each.
I can compare two verification strategies and judge which is more reliable, with a reason.
I can back my verdicts with evidence from a trusted source.

terms.definition: A fixed set of steps applied the same way to every output.
Your conclusion on a claim: verified, false, or unclear.
The trusted-source information that backs your verdict.
Sources that do not copy each other, so they are unlikely to share the same error.
A method you can trust to give the right result repeatedly.

sections.heading: A routine keeps you fair
body: When you check many outputs, it is tempting to judge each one by how confident it sounds. A verification [[routine]] stops that: the same fixed steps apply to every output, so a slick output gets no easy pass.

Our routine has four steps - isolate the claim, pick an independent trusted source, compare, and record a verdict. The [[verdict]] can be verified, false, or unclear, and 'unclear' is an honest answer when the evidence is not there.

sections.heading: Not all checks are equally reliable
body: A single-source check is quick, but if that one source is wrong or out of date, your verdict is wrong too. A two-source cross-check is slower but far harder to fool, because two [[independent sources]] rarely share the same mistake.

Judging which strategy is more [[reliable]] means weighing speed against confidence and asking a sharp question: could these sources fail together? The more independent they are, the more you can trust their agreement.

sections.label: Hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Work in groups with roles: claim-isolator, source-checker, verdict-recorder, reporter. Run the routine on the whole batch, then compare two strategies on a tricky output.
items: Copy the four routine steps onto your sheet.
For each output, isolate the claim and pick a trusted source.
Compare and record a verdict with its evidence.
Choose one tricky output and check it single-source, then two-source.
Judge which strategy is more reliable and why.
For one false output, write the harm and the check that de-risks it.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which verdict was hardest to reach, and what made it hard?
When is the slower two-source check worth the extra time?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: State which verification strategy you would use and the trade-off you accept.
Note one responsible-use habit this workshop reinforced.

questions.prompt: Your group is handed a new suspect output. Put the four steps of the verification routine in the order the lesson uses.

items.text: Isolate the exact claim the output is making.
Pick a trusted source that is independent of the AI.
Compare the claim with what that source says.
Record the verdict: verified, false or unclear.

feedback.correct: Running the same fixed steps on every output is what stops a slick answer getting an easy pass.
feedback.incorrect: The routine gathers evidence before it judges: isolate the claim, choose an independent source, compare, and only then record the verdict.

questions.prompt: Your group has run the routine on four outputs. Match what the source-checker found to the verdict the recorder should write.

left.text: The official site gives the same tower height as the output.
The official site gives a different opening date from the output.
No trusted source on the reference sheet mentions the claim at all.
Two sites agree, but the second says its figures were taken from the first.

right.text: Verified - an independent trusted source agrees with the claim.
False - a trusted source contradicts the claim.
Unclear - no source covers it, so there is no evidence either way.
Count it as one source - they are not independent, so they could share the same error.
Verified - the output sounded confident and nothing has contradicted it.

feedback.correct: Every verdict is tied to what the evidence showed - including the honest 'unclear' and the copied source that only looks like two.
feedback.incorrect: A verdict reports what the trusted source showed: agreement, contradiction, no evidence at all, or sources that copy each other and therefore count as one.

questions.prompt: Your group checks the claim "the festival first ran in 1998". None of the trusted sources on the reference sheet mention the festival's first year. What should the verdict-recorder write, and why?

options.text: Verified - nothing contradicted the claim, so it stands.
False - if a trusted source does not mention it, the claim must be made up.
Unclear - no trusted source covers this claim, so there is no evidence either way.
Verified - the output gave the year with no hesitation, and confident claims are usually right.

feedback.correct: 'Unclear' is an honest verdict: it records that the evidence is missing instead of inventing a judgement.
feedback.incorrect: Missing evidence is not proof that a claim is false, and it is not permission to pass it either - the routine lets you record 'unclear'.

questions.prompt: Your group has ten outputs and limited time, so you will only cross-check some of them with a second source. Which of these are sound reasons for spending the extra time on a particular output? Select all that apply.

options.text: Getting this claim wrong would matter to the people who read it, so confidence is worth more than speed here.
The one source you used could be out of date, so a single check might miss an error.
The output sounds confident and polished, so it needs less checking than the others.
The second source you would add is run by the same organisation as the first.
Your group has spare time, and spare time is what makes a check reliable.

feedback.correct: You spend the extra time where a wrong verdict would cost most, or where one source could quietly be wrong.
feedback.incorrect: Choose by what is at stake and by how the first source could fail - not by how confident the output sounds, and not by adding a source that would fail alongside the first.

questions.prompt: Complete the trade-off from the lab: a single-source check is ___, but your verdict is wrong if that one source is wrong; a two-source cross-check is ___, yet much harder to fool because the two sources are ___ of each other.
blanks: the two sources are ___ of each other

feedback.correct: That is the judgement in one line: you trade speed for confidence, and the confidence comes from independence.
feedback.incorrect: The cross-check costs time and buys reliability - two sources that do not copy each other rarely make the same mistake.

formative.targets: Grade 5 Advanced: explains misinformation risks and proposes verification strategies
formative.check: Completed verification workshop sheet with verdicts and evidence for a batch, plus a reasoned comparison of two strategies
formative.successCriteria: Applies the routine to reach evidence-based verdicts and judges which verification strategy is more reliable with a reason.
formative.evidence: Workshop sheet with per-output verdicts + strategy comparison and judgement.
